disease_info: Adjustment Disorder is characterized by the development of emotional or behavioral disturbances within three months of an identifiable psychosocial stressor, with distress out of proportion to the severity or intensity of the stressor and/or significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. The presentation is heterogeneous and can include anxious, depressed, or mixed emotional features, as well as maladaptive behavioral responses such as withdrawal, conflict, or decline in role performance. By definition, the disturbance does not represent normal bereavement, does not meet criteria for another mental disorder, and symptoms do not persist for more than six months after the stressor or its consequences have ended. It is often seen in the context of life transitions, interpersonal conflicts, health problems, or occupational stress, and is distinguished from more severe mood or anxiety disorders by its time-limited, stressor-linked course and relatively circumscribed impairment.

narrative.personality: Paul is a quietly introspective, methodical historian who finds comfort in routine, solitary hobbies, and careful financial planning.
narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Paul’s freelance work had been gradually shrinking as several regional journals cut budgets and the historical society he collaborated with shifted to in‑house staff, but he reassured himself he could make do by tightening expenses. The turning point came when his largest ongoing contract for digitizing a private Gettysburg collection was abruptly cancelled after the donor redirected funds, leaving him with a sudden and substantial drop in income and no clear replacement project. For someone who has long used meticulous budgeting, cataloging, and quiet, structured work as anchors after his divorce, the loss of this contract felt like a direct threat to both his financial stability and his identity as a valued historian, and over the following month he became increasingly preoccupied with the possibility of depleting his savings, stalling out professionally, and having to sell family heirlooms or his home. As these worries began to interfere with his ability to concentrate on smaller projects, maintain his usual volunteer archival work, and enjoy his solitary walks and gardening, a friend from the historical society urged him to see a psychiatrist, prompting him to seek help when he realized the stress around this setback was starting to disrupt his daily functioning.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since I lost my main contract, I feel like I’m not handling the stress in a normal way and it’s starting to affect how I function day to day.”

narrative.personality: Amy is a highly organized, routine‑oriented woman who takes pride in precision, reliability, and keeping her environment and responsibilities meticulously ordered.
narrative.stressor: Amy had managed her health fairly well into her mid‑80s, structuring her days around work at the senior center, church, and familiar home routines, when she experienced a sudden fall on her front steps that resulted in a hip fracture and brief hospitalization. Although the surgery went well, she was told she would need to use a walker for several months and cut back significantly on her front‑desk duties, and her husband and adult children began gently insisting she not live alone at home during her recovery. For someone who has built her identity around independence, punctuality, and being the dependable point‑person at the senior center, the abrupt loss of mobility and control over her schedule—with others now rearranging her medications, appointments, and even her kitchen—felt deeply unsettling, and over the next month she struggled to reconcile the imposed changes with her need for order and self‑reliance, leading her to increasingly rigid and strained attempts to maintain her old routines. When staff at the senior center noticed that her distress about minor scheduling changes and perceived mistakes was escalating and beginning to interfere with her ability to enjoy her hobbies and interact calmly with others, her primary care physician recommended a psychiatric evaluation to help her adjust to the health-related changes.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Since I broke my hip and everyone started changing my routines, I just haven’t been coping with all the stress the way I usually can.”

narrative.personality: Eric is a competitive, structure‑driven professional who thrives on clear goals, order, and high performance, balancing intense work focus with organized social and athletic pursuits.
narrative.stressor: Eric had carefully mapped out both his career trajectory toward a security manager role and a stable home life with his wife, with shared routines around church, soccer, and extended family gatherings, when his wife disclosed that she was unexpectedly pregnant at the same time she was considering relocating closer to her family for a job opportunity. The news collided with his tightly controlled financial planning and performance goals, as he worried about affording childcare, potentially starting over at a new casino, and losing the familiar support network and routines he believes keep him on track. Over the subsequent month, ongoing, unresolved conversations with his wife about whether to move, how to manage their schedules, and what compromises each would make began to feel like a constant pressure; at work he found himself increasingly preoccupied with fears of failing as a provider and partner, while at home he reacted to minor disagreements with an intensity that surprised even him, straining their relationship further. When his supervisor informally noted that he seemed unusually distracted on shift and his wife expressed concern that his stress over these changes was starting to dominate their interactions and decisions, Eric agreed to see a psychiatrist, recognizing that his way of responding to the situation was no longer constructive and was impairing both his performance and family life.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since my wife told me about the pregnancy and possible move, I feel like I’m reacting to the stress all wrong and it’s starting to mess up my work and home life.”
